title: Family of footballer who died from cardiac arrest ‘shocked, disappointed’ as FA opposes coroner’s wishes
content:
The family of Adam Ankers, the 17-year-old footballer who died from sudden cardiac arrest, say they are “disappointed and shocked” after learning that the Football Association is opposing a coroner’s wishes for coaches and referees to receive mandatory training aimed at preventing future deaths.

Ankers, who played for the Wycombe Wanderers foundation team, collapsed during a game in January 2024, leading to a coroner writing to the FA to express her concerns that the sport was not doing enough to tackle the risks of players suffering cardiac arrest.

Valerie Charbit, assistant coroner of west London, is putting together a Prevention of Future Deaths (PFD) report in which she addresses her concerns that “the FA’s SCA (sudden cardiac arrest) training was not more widely disseminated or mandatory for all grassroots football coaches and referees.”

However, it emerged during a hearing on Tuesday that the FA’s lawyers had written to Charbit to ask her to “refrain” from filing a report in support of “blanket mandatory requirements.” The coroner told Tuesday’s hearing she had carefully considered the FA’s submission but would deliver her report, as planned, regardless of the objections.

“We feel like the FA have led us up the garden path,” Alastair, Ankers’ father, said after the hearing. “During the inquest (while the inquest was ongoing), the FA’s representatives told us more than once that the FA wanted to work with us, to help us to keep other children safe, and make sure nothing like this would ever happen again.

“We’re disappointed and shocked that, when it came to it, their written submission basically says they don’t accept the coroner’s findings, they don’t feel they should be named in the Prevention of Future Deaths report, and they don’t feel there is much else they need to do.”

The 11-page submission, seen by The Athletic, argues that the FA is already trying to strengthen and increase its SCA training, but that “there are likely to be unintended adverse consequences if the courses were made mandatory.”

It goes on to note that “a mandatory requirement would need to be implemented for more than 185,000 coaches across more than 100,000 clubs at grassroots level.”

Addressing the FA’s points, the coroner responded by stating that her own conclusions “outweighed the concerns” of English football’s governing body, taking into account “the number of young lives that could be saved if that training was, in fact, conducted by many more people.”

In Ankers’ case, nobody knew that the teenager was suffering from a genetic heart condition known as ARVC (arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy). His inquest heard that the referee had not undertaken SCA training and, despite a defibrillator being brought to the scene, the attempts to revive Ankers did not start until paramedics arrived. Crucially, the emergency 999 call handler at South Central Ambulance Service did not recognise the symptoms of cardiac arrest and gave the wrong advice over the telephone. The coroner described it as a “missed opportunity” that “more than minimally” contributed to his death.

Ankers’ family have backed the coroner’s call for referees to receive mandatory SCA training. However, the FA asked the coroner to “reconsider” this proposal, indicating that there might be safeguarding concerns for younger referees, as well as the possibility that it would put off some people from wanting to officiate matches.

“Referees have not previously been allocated responsibility for responding to serious health issues because of their age and limited, often challenging role,” states the FA’s written submission. “A significant proportion of referees are children: refereeing is permitted from the age of 14 and approximately 40 per cent of the nearly 40,000 FA-registered referees are under the age of 18.”

As well as stating that “children should not be made responsible for directing urgent first-aid,” the FA’s submission goes to say that a mandatory requirement “would be likely to deter participation, increasing the existing challenges regarding the number and retention of referees, which are already adversely impacting grassroots football.”

“I disagree,” Charbit said at Tuesday’s hearing. “I consider it important that the responsibility for first-aid lies with all ages in society and outweighs any concerns that this will effectively stop them from becoming referees.”

The most alarming part for the Ankers family is that the coroner’s report can make recommendations but will not, on its own, compel the relevant organisations to make changes. The FA says it is reviewing all the findings.

In their own submissions, the Ankers family noted there had been other tragedies in football involving players colliding with concrete perimeter walls and that, despite warnings from a coroner in 2015, many grounds continued to have potentially dangerous walls.

The family asked the coroner to note the FA’s approach and cited the tragic case last year of 21-year-old Billy Vigar, a former Arsenal academy player, who died from his injuries after colliding with a pitch-side wall during a game for Chichester City at the ground of Wingate & Finchley in North London. The FA is now holding a safety review.

An FA spokesperson told the The Athletic: “We were deeply saddened to learn of the tragic passing of Adam Ankers and our thoughts remain with his family and loved ones. We have supported the coroner throughout the inquest, and we will fully review their findings and recommendations.”

In Ankers’ case, it remains to be seen whether the FA will adhere to the family’s wishes. The latest evidence, however, suggests doubt that training will become mandatory for either coaches or referees.

“It seems to us that they (the FA) wanted to get their name off the coroner’s report for the sake of their reputation,” said Alastair. “Yet this shouldn’t be about reputational damage. It isn’t about pointing fingers of blame. It’s about trying to prevent more young people from dying and other families being devastated.”
